stories.title: Law Firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee Takes 11K SF at 7 World Trade Center
stories.excerpt: Washington D.C.-based law firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee is establishing a new office in New York City. The firm, which specializes in high stakes trials, investigations and crisis management, has inked an 11,167-square-foot lease on the 34th floor of 7 World Trade Center, developer and landlord Silverstein Properties announced Monday. Silverstein did not disclose the length of the lease or the asking rent. However, a source close to the deal noted asking rents in the building range from $100 to $150 per square foot. The average asking rent for Class A office space at the World Trade Center was $78.37 per square foot during the second quarter of 2026, according to Colliers data. “We are excited to welcome our teams and our clients into our new Manhattan office later this year,” Jeannie Rhee, managing partner of Dunn Isaacson Rhee, said in a statement. “7 World Trade Center offers the ideal combination of thoughtful design, functionality, and a premier location in the heart of the Financial District and a stone’s throw to the Southern District of New York courthouse.” Dunn Isaacson Rhee will relocate from 11 Park Place, also in the Financial District. It’s unclear when the firm will make the move. Dunn Isaacson Rhee did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. Lisa Ann Pollakowski, Cory Gahr and Richard Plehn from Lee & Associates represented the tenant in the deal, while Silverstein was represented in-house by Keith A. Cody, Gordon Hough and Harlan Strader, as well as by CBRE’s MaryAnn Tighe. Lee & Associates did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. “Dunn Isaacson Rhee represents the caliber of organization that continues to define 7 World Trade Center as one of Downtown Manhattan’s premier office destinations,” Silverstein’s Cody said in a statement. “Today’s leading firms are seeking workplaces that reflect their brand, support their people and provide an exceptional experience for their clients. bullets: Dunn Isaacson Rhee (D.C. law firm) leases 11.2K SF at 7 World Trade, Manhattan
Asking rents $100–$150/SF vs. WTC average $78.37/SF in Q2 2026; premium 27–91%
Office tenant demand signals Financial District desirability despite pricing above submarket norm
stories.summary: Washington D.C.-based law firm Dunn Isaacson Rhee signed an 11,167-SF lease on the 34th floor of 7 World Trade Center in Lower Manhattan at asking rents between $100–$150/SF, significantly above the World Trade Center's Q2 2026 Class A average of $78.37/SF. The firm is establishing a new NYC office to serve high-stakes litigation and crisis management clients. Silverstein Properties' flagship asset continues to attract premium tenants despite broader Manhattan office headwinds.
stories.impact: Law firm expansion into NYC signals confidence in Financial District and WTC's tenant appeal, but premium rents ($27–72/SF above submarket) underscore bifurcated office market: Class A trophy assets command pricing power while secondary stock languishes. This does NOT improve residential demand or supply dynamics in Lower Manhattan directly, but sustained office vitality may support ancillary retail and hospitality that indirectly benefits mixed-use residential conversions.

stories.title: Alliance for Downtown New York Takes 14K SF at 42 Broadway
stories.excerpt: Nonprofit group Alliance For Downtown New York has expanded its Lower Manhattan footprint to 42 Broadway. The Downtown Alliance, which manages the area’s business improvement district, secured a 14,420-square-foot lease at the Financial District tower, according to a recent CBRE office market report. The Downtown Alliance plans to relocate its operations division to the 22-story office building, a spokesperson for the nonprofit told CO. The nonprofit’s corporate headquarters remain housed roughly three blocks north at Silverstein Properties’ 120 Broadway. JLL’s John Wheeler and his team at JLL represented the tenant in the negotiations. A spokesperson for the team did not respond immediately to a request for comment. The lease terms were not disclosed, but office asking rents in Lower Manhattan averaged $61.91 per square foot in July, according to the CBRE report. A spokesperson for the landlord, Avi Schron‘s Cammeby’s International Group, confirmed the recent transaction to CO, adding that the space is still under construction. It was not immediately clear whether Cammeby’s International Group worked with any outside brokers. Cammeby’s 42 Broadway is located near the intersection of Broadway and Morris Street. Appellate service organization Office of the Appellate Defender relocated there in November, joining a tenant roster that includes office suite provider TKO Suites, chiropractor Prestige Health and Wellness, dental practice DDS Group and cafe Gregorys Coffee. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Alliance for Downtown NY relocates ops to 42 Broadway, 14.4K SF lease in Financial District
Lower Manhattan office rents $61.91/SF (July); BID expansion suggests neighborhood stabilization
Nonprofit consolidation within 3-block radius (120 Broadway HQ remains) reinforces downtown institutional anchoring
stories.summary: The Alliance for Downtown New York (the Financial District's business improvement district) leased 14,420 SF at 42 Broadway to relocate its operations division, while maintaining headquarters at Silverstein's 120 Broadway three blocks north. Office asking rents in Lower Manhattan averaged $61.91/SF in July, per CBRE. The transaction was brokered by JLL; landlord Cammeby's International Group confirmed the deal, with space still under construction.
stories.impact: BID expansion and operational consolidation in Lower Manhattan signals institutional confidence in Financial District recovery and suggests sustained capital flowing into downtown office recovery, but the submarket's lower average rent ($61.91/SF) versus WTC flagship ($78.37/SF) indicates severe flight-to-quality and secondary-asset distress. For multifamily, this affirms Financial District office stabilization that could support mixed-use and residential conversions targeting affluent financial services workers, but primary demand is still concentrated in trophy assets, not broad-based neighborhood revival.

stories.title: New York’s Rent Freeze Was Only An Aftershock. This 2019 Law Was The Quake.
stories.excerpt: Jose Tur owns two rent-stabilized rental buildings in Manhattan’s Washington Heights with a total of 45 units. The properties have been in his family for over 30 years, and the mortgages are fully paid off. But Tur tells Commercial Observer that despite this, while he’s reluctant to give an exact number, “more than two or three” units have been sitting empty for an average of over two years. That’s because, according to Tur’s estimates, it would cost anywhere from $30,000 to $60,000 per unit to return them to a livable state, and that’s money he can’t justify spending in return for the stabilized rent amounts in today’s environment. “Some of them require more work than others, but for the ones that need significant work — and I mean baseline, just to get them up to livable standards — we’re talking $30,000 minimum,” said Tur, who has testified about these financial challenges to New York City’s Rent Guidelines Board (RGB). “[Oftentimes] the plumbing’s really old because a tenant has lived there for 10 to 15 years, and you have to do the electrical and then lead abatement, which really increases the tally on the job.” Tur says that the $30,000 estimate is before taking into account more cosmetic fixes like cabinets, tiles and so forth, meaning the total is often closer to $60,000 for a one-bedroom apartment. Given all this, the fate of his currently empty apartments is uncertain. With no financial relief in sight, it is likely the units will not be lived in again for the foreseeable future, removed from the rolls of New York’s livable spaces — and from Tur’s income-producing properties — as if they had never existed. The RGB approved a freeze on rent increases for one- and two-year leases for the city’s rent-stabilized apartments in June for lease terms beginning on Oct. 1 or later. bullets: NYC rent-stabilized owner (45-unit Manhattan portfolio) reports 2+ units vacant 2+ years due to economics
Rehabilitation costs $30K–$60K/unit minimum; stabilized rents cannot justify capex ROI under 2019 rent-control law
Systemic capital decay and unit withdrawal in stabilized stock signals hidden supply loss in NYC rental market
stories.summary: A Manhattan rent-stabilized landlord with a fully paid-off, 30-year family property reports more than two of his 45 units have sat empty for over two years. He estimates rehabilitation costs of $30K–$60K per unit (plumbing, electrical, lead abatement) that cannot be economically justified by the regulated rents allowed under New York's 2019 rent-control regime. The landlord has testified to the Rent Guidelines Board that these dynamics prevent unit return and maintenance investment.
stories.impact: Rent-stabilized buildings are withdrawing units from the market via deliberate vacancy rather than reinvest—a form of supply loss invisible in delivery data. This artificially inflates available unstabilized-unit scarcity and supports market-rate rents in Manhattan's core, creating favorable underwriting for new market-rate multifamily development. However, the underlying signal is regulatory damage to small landlord capital structure, which may depress future Manhattan acquisition prices for stabilized portfolios and redirect development capital toward unregulated markets (Bronx, Queens, outer boroughs) where returns are less constrained.

stories.title: Local Developer Plans to Build a School at 1000 University Avenue in the Bronx
stories.excerpt: School is in session in the Bronx, or at least it will be. Kiumarz Geula, principal of real estate development firm Pillar Property Management, has filed plans with the New York City Department of Buildings (DOB) to build a seven-story school building at 1000 University Avenue in the Highbridge neighborhood of the Bronx. The plans were filed with the DOB on Aug. 5. Geula did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s request for comment. Jonathan Imani of IMC Architecture, the registered architect on the project, also did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. The DOB plans have few details about the scope of the work coming to the vacant Bronx property. The plans call for the construction of a 64,366-square-foot, 108-foot tall building with a cafeteria and recreation space. No other details are available. Pillar Property Management isn’t the only developer planning to bring a new school building to the Bronx. In June, Apex Development Group and Knickpoint Ventures secured a $60 million debt package to acquire and build a charter school at 1780 East Tremont Avenue, Commercial Observer reported at the time. Ripco Real Estate’s James Murad, who arranged the financing for that deal, told CO at the time that the project reflects “the growing demand for high-quality educational facilities in underserved communities and the continued appeal of mission-driven real estate investments.” Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Pillar Property Management (Kiumarz Geula) files plans for 64.4K SF school at 1000 University Ave, Bronx Highbridge
Seven-story institutional use; Apex/Knickpoint secured $60M debt for charter school on East Tremont same quarter
Dual charter-school pipeline signals institutional capital and rezoning/entitlement momentum in outer-borough development
stories.summary: Real estate developer Kiumarz Geula's firm Pillar Property Management filed plans with NYC Department of Buildings on August 5 to construct a 64,366-SF, 108-foot tall school building with cafeteria and recreation space at 1000 University Avenue in Bronx Highbridge. The filing coincides with competitor Apex Development Group and Knickpoint Ventures securing $60 million debt financing for a charter school at 1780 East Tremont Avenue in the Bronx in June, indicating a sector-wide pivot to education real estate in the borough.
stories.impact: Charter school institutional pipeline in the Bronx reflects capital availability, favorable local zoning/entitlement environment, and demographic-driven demand for educational facilities. This signals broader confidence in outer-borough submarkets and may precede residential demand surge (families relocating for school choice, workforce growth around institutional anchors). Multifamily developers should monitor Highbridge and East Tremont for next-generation residential absorption and rent growth, particularly family-oriented two- and three-bedroom units; institutional anchors typically improve neighborhood positioning for residential underwriting.

stories.title: Gencom Divides Into Two Business Lines With Leadership Promotions
stories.excerpt: Real estate investment firm Gencom is reorganizing into two different business lines, with new hires and promotions to match. The reorganization splits the firm, which has $8 billion in assets under management, into Gencom Capital and Gencom Real Estate, with CEO and founder Karim Alibhai continuing to steer both ships, according to Gencom. Gencom operates up to 6,000 hotel rooms nationwide, including brands like Ritz-Carlton, Rosewood, Auberge Resorts Collection, Fairmont, Hyatt and Marriott. “Successful real estate platforms are built by combining disciplined investing with exceptional execution,” Alibhai said in a statement. “As Gencom continues to grow, this evolution strengthens our leadership, sharpens accountability and positions us to capitalize on the opportunities ahead while continuing to deliver outstanding outcomes for our investors and partners.” Gencom Capital will be led by Chief Investment Officer Alessandro Colantonio, who will handle capital markets, portfolio management and capital allocation. Newly promoted managing directors include Ignasi Puig, who will handle acquisitions and investments; Peter Trujillo, who will be responsible for corporate investments; and Blythe Pierre-Louis, who will manage special situations. Meanwhile, Donald McGregor was promoted to president of Gencom Real Estate and will oversee development, construction and asset management. Shaun Johnston was also promoted to head of portfolio finance and accounting and will report directly to McGregor. Jake Lynch was hired as senior vice president of asset management for Gencom Real Estate. “As we continue to grow, we are building a team with the expertise to create value at every stage of the investment lifecycle,” McGregor said in a statement. “Jake is a terrific addition to the Gencom Real Estate platform, and Shaun’s promotion reflects the depth of talent we have developed within the firm. bullets: Gencom ($8B AUM) reorganizes into Gencom Capital and Gencom Real Estate; CEO Karim Alibhai remains
Firm operates 6K hotel rooms nationwide (Ritz-Carlton, Hyatt, Marriott, Fairmont brands)
Leadership restructuring signals platform maturation and capital-discipline pivot; no impact on multifamily supply/demand
stories.summary: Real estate investment and hospitality firm Gencom, which manages $8 billion in assets, restructured into two standalone business lines: Gencom Capital (led by Chief Investment Officer Alessandro Colantonio, handling capital markets and portfolio management) and Gencom Real Estate, with CEO and founder Karim Alibhai remaining in charge of both. The firm operates approximately 6,000 hotel rooms under premium brands including Ritz-Carlton, Rosewood, Hyatt, and Marriott.
stories.impact: Gencom's reorganization is primarily a hospitality-sector governance event; the firm's $8B portfolio and hotel-focused asset base do not directly affect multifamily development supply, demand, capital availability, or cost. No material relevance to apartment development markets.
